summary: This document describes a header field, SIO-Label, for Internet email that conveys the sensitivity of a message. It can carry a human-readable display marking, a structured security label, or both. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Some letters are marked secret or for staff only. This describes a way to put that kind of marking on an email so computers and people both see it.

subtitle: A header field to mark email messages with sensitivity information for display and policy handling.

tldr.problem: Organizations need to label email messages with their sensitivity level (e.g., Confidential, Internal Use Only) so people and mail systems know how to handle them. Many organizations add labels as text in the subject or message body, but this is informal and lacks interoperability. Some systems use proprietary header fields, creating incompatibility.
tldr.mechanism: This specification defines two header fields: SIO-Label conveys the sensitivity of a message as a display marking (text), foreground and background colors, and optionally a structured security label (ESS, X.411, or XML format); SIO-Label-History records changes made to the label as the message passes through the mail system.
tldr.outcome: Mail systems can now standardly communicate message sensitivity in a format that both human users and automated systems can recognize, enabling consistent display of sensitivity markings, policy-based message handling, and audit trails of label changes.

facts.label: Structured label formats
facts.value: ESS, X.411, XML, or custom URI

facts.label: Color formats
facts.value: Hex RGB (#rrggbb) or CSS named colors

today: RFC 7444 is an Informational specification that registers the SIO-Label and SIO-Label-History header fields in the Provisional Message Header Field Registry. The header fields remain useful for organizations needing to communicate message sensitivity, particularly in government, military, and regulated business environments. However, broad email deployment remains limited, and many organizations continue to use inline markings or proprietary headers. The specification supports but does not require signature-based binding of labels to messages.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A security label is a structured representation of the sensitivity of information. Organizations that operate under information classification rules—such as government, military, and sensitive corporate networks—use security labels to control who can access what information. A display marking is the human-readable version, such as "CONFIDENTIAL" or "INTERNAL USE ONLY."

Internet email messages frequently need to carry sensitivity information, but standards for doing so have been missing. Many organizations currently place the sensitivity marking as plain text in the Subject line or at the start and end of the message body, a practice known as inline sensitivity markings (FLOT/LLOT markings). Some mail systems use non-standard header fields like X-X411.

This specification defines a standard header field, SIO-Label, to convey the sensitivity of an email message as a whole. It can carry a display marking (textual), foreground and background colors for displaying the marking, and/or a structured security label (in ESS, X.411, or XML format). The specification also defines SIO-Label-History to record changes made to the label as the message traverses the mail system.
sections.eli5: Email should be marked with how secret it is, like a letter stamped confidential. This describes a standard way to add that mark to any email so mail programs and people see it.

sections.title: How SIO-Label Is Used
sections.content:
A Mail User Agent (MUA) composing a message can offer the user a menu of sensitivities to choose from and insert the corresponding display marking, colors, and security label into the SIO-Label header. Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs) and Mail Delivery Agents (MDAs) can then examine the header to decide whether to accept, forward, or modify the message. A mail agent handling the label MAY add an SIO-Label-History header to record the change.

When displaying the message, a receiving MUA SHALL prominently display the marking (either the one conveyed in the header or one generated locally from the label and a security policy) using the specified foreground and background colors. MUAs can also use the sensitivity information to organize messages in local storage or make other handling decisions, though they are not expected to enforce authorization based on the label.

This approach supports environments where messages need clear sensitivity indicators visible to both automated systems and users. Unlike Enhanced Security Services for S/MIME (which securely binds labels to content through digital signatures), this simple mechanism assumes message signing is not necessary.
sections.eli5: When you write an email, you pick how secret it is. The mail system sees that marking and shows it to the person who reads it. If the mail system changes the marking, it keeps track of who changed it and when.

sections.title: The SIO-Label Header Field
sections.content:
The SIO-Label header field contains a sequence of parameters separated by semicolons, following the syntax defined in RFC 2231.

The marking parameter is the human-readable sensitivity label as a text string (e.g., "EXAMPLE CONFIDENTIAL"). It SHOULD generally be present. The fgcolor and bgcolor parameters specify foreground and background colors for displaying the marking, as either RGB hex values (e.g., "#ff0000" for red) or CSS color names (e.g., "red", "blue", "white"). Default colors are black text on white background. These color parameters are required if marking is present.

The type parameter is a quoted string indicating the format and encoding of the label parameter. Four type values are defined: ":ess" for base64-encoded ESS security labels (from RFC 2634); ":x411" for base64-encoded X.411 security labels; ":xml" for base64-encoded XML security labels; or a URI denoting a custom type. The label parameter contains the encoded structured security label. The type and label parameters must appear together, or both must be absent.

A message must contain zero or one SIO-Label header field. The header field must contain either a marking parameter or both type and label parameters (or both marking and label).
sections.eli5: The header has a marking (like the word Confidential), colors (like black and red), and optionally a structured label (a computer-readable format of the same sensitivity). All parts are optional as long as there is something there.

sections.title: The SIO-Label-History Header Field
sections.content:
The SIO-Label-History header field is a trace header (as defined in RFC 5322) that records changes made to the SIO-Label header. Each SIO-Label-History entry tracks one modification. Multiple SIO-Label-History headers may appear; new entries should be inserted immediately before existing ones (newest first).

Each history entry must contain the change parameter ("add", "replace", or "delete"), changed-by (identifying the mail agent that made the change), and changed-at (a date-time when the change was made). An optional changed-comment may provide context.

When the change is "add", the entry records the new-marking, new-fgcolor, new-bgcolor, new-type, and new-label (the label information added). When the change is "replace", it records both the old and new values. When the change is "delete", it records the old values being removed. This allows mail administrators and users to audit how sensitivity labels have been modified as messages pass through the system.
sections.eli5: When a mail server changes the sensitivity marking, it writes down who changed it, when, and what the old and new markings are. This makes an audit trail so you can see who touched the marking and when.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Sensitive information should be appropriately protected by transport-level security, authentication, and authorization mechanisms, independent of sensitivity labels. The label itself does not provide protection; it is merely an expression of sensitivity for handling decisions and display purposes.

The marking itself might be sensitive (e.g., "BLACK PROJECT RESTRICTED" discloses the existence of a classified project). The label applies to the entire message (header and body together), not to individual MIME parts, reflecting a design choice favoring simplicity over complexity.

Mail systems using the header to make authorization decisions should authenticate the sending entity and verify that the label authenticity. However, unlike ESS, this mechanism provides no message-signing services and hence no secure binding of the label to the message content, no content integrity protection, and no non-repudiation. It is intended for environments where message signing is not necessary.

The SIO-Label-History header may contain sensitive information (e.g., revealing previous classification levels) and should be removed when its inclusion would cause inappropriate disclosure. The specification recommends that agents verify consistency between the security label and display marking, rejecting messages with inconsistent values.
sections.eli5: The marking is just information; it does not protect the message by itself. Real security needs encryption and authentication. The marking can itself be secret, so you might remove the history headers before sending the message to someone outside your organization.
